subject: English
period_schedule_display:
Period schedule:
  Row 1: 40 minutes × 11 periods = 440 minutes
Total: 11 periods · 7h 20min

periods.activity_title: First Encounter: Reading the Chandrayaan Story Aloud

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us read (pp.118–121): read the Chandrayaan narrative aloud together.

time_bands.activity: Open to pp.118–119. Ask children what they notice about the title 'Chandrayaan' and invite a quick oral prediction about what the story might be about. Accept all responses warmly.

Let us read ("read-aloud of the Chandrayaan narrative, pp.118–121"). Teacher reads the full narrative with expression, pausing at dialogue between Rani, Pratik, and Nandini Aunty so children can follow in their books.
Shared re-reading: teacher reads a paragraph, children echo it aloud together, paying attention to names — Rani, Pratik, Vivaan, Nandini Aunty — and key facts such as the launch and landing dates.
Brief whole-class discussion: What was Rani curious about? What did Nandini Aunty explain? Accept oral answers freely; no written response is required at this point.

periods.teacher_notes: Children at Grade III may be unfamiliar with space-mission vocabulary; write 'rocket', 'Chandrayaan', 'launched' and 'landed' on the board before reading so children can follow along without stopping. Emphasise the warm, curious tone of the story — Rani's habit of asking questions is the emotional heart of the narrative and will anchor later discussion.
materials: Board and chalk/marker for key vocabulary

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us think — A (p.122): answer five comprehension questions about the story.

time_bands.activity: Brief re-read aloud of the story's central episode (pp.119–121, Nandini Aunty's explanation) to refresh the content before moving into questions.

Let us think — A, questions 1–3 (p.122): ("How do we know Rani was curious? What did Pratik say? Who was Nandini Aunty?"). Teacher poses each question orally; children discuss in pairs, then share answers aloud before the class agrees on a response.

Let us think — A, questions 4–5 (p.122): ("What do Chandra and Yaan mean? Complete: Chandrayaan-3 landed on the Moon on ___."). Children write the fill-in answer in their notebooks; teacher circulates and supports.
Whole-class share-out: invite two or three children to read their answers aloud. Confirm the landing date (23 August 2023) and the meanings of 'Chandra' (Moon) and 'Yaan' (vehicle) on the board.

periods.teacher_notes: Having read the narrative together, children should be able to cite Rani's constant questioning as evidence of curiosity — guide them to point to specific moments in the text rather than offering general answers. The fill-in question about the landing date is factual and exact; accept only '23 August 2023' or equivalent.

periods.activity_title: Imagining the Moon: Think and Say

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us think — B (p.122): list 10 items you would take for 10 days on the Moon.

time_bands.activity: Teacher sets the imaginative context: Nandini Aunty told Rani she might one day go to the Moon. Ask children: 'If scientists invited YOU to spend 10 days on the Moon, what would you need?' Give children a moment to think silently and jot ideas in their notebooks.

Let us think — B ("10-item packing list for the Moon, p.122"): children work in pairs to build a shared list of 10 items, discussing each choice. Teacher moves between pairs, asking guiding questions such as 'Will there be air on the Moon?' and 'What will you eat?'
Pairs share their lists with the class. Teacher collects items on the board, grouping them into categories (food, air/breathing, clothing, equipment). Children note any item they had not thought of.
Quick whole-class reflection: which item appeared on almost every list? Why? Children answer orally in one or two sentences.

periods.teacher_notes: The packing-list task is an imaginative extension of Nandini Aunty's conversation with Rani and Pratik; encourage children to think practically (oxygen, food, water) as well as creatively. Avoid correcting 'impossible' items harshly — the goal is expansive oral reasoning, not scientific accuracy at this stage.

periods.activity_title: Sharing Travel Experiences: Let Us Speak

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us speak (p.123): share a personal experience of travelling to a far-off place.

time_bands.activity: Teacher connects to the story: Chandrayaan travelled the enormous distance between Earth and the Moon. Ask children whether they have ever made a long journey — by train, bus, or any vehicle. Invite two quick hands-up responses.

Let us speak ("share a personal travel experience, p.123"): each child spends a quiet moment recalling a trip to a far-off place. If they have not travelled far themselves, they think of a story an elder at home has shared. Teacher circulates, gently prompting shy children with 'Where did you go? How did you travel? What did you see?'

Children take turns sharing their experience with the class in three to four sentences. Teacher models active listening and briefly asks one follow-up question per speaker to extend the oral response (e.g. 'Was the journey exciting or tiring?').

Whole-class close: teacher draws a quick parallel — just as people travel far on Earth, Chandrayaan made the longest journey of all. Children repeat: 'Chandrayaan travelled from Earth all the way to the Moon!'

periods.teacher_notes: The speaking task is directly inspired by the story's theme of distance — Chandrayaan's journey to the Moon mirrors a long journey a child or family elder has made. Children who have not travelled far should not feel excluded; family members' stories are equally valid and are explicitly invited by the task.

periods.activity_title: Consonant Blends in Writing: sk, sw, sp, st

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us write — A (p.125): fill blanks by forming words with blends sk, sw, sp, st.

time_bands.activity: Write the four blends — sk, sw, sp, st — on the board. Teacher says each blend clearly and children repeat chorally. Brainstorm one example word per blend together (e.g. sky, swim, spin, stop) and write them beside the blend.

Read the model sentence from the textbook aloud: 'There are swings in the park' — children identify the blend 'sw' in 'swings'. Teacher explains how a blend prefix joins to a root to make a complete word.

Let us write — A ("consonant-blend fill-in sentences, p.125"): children attempt each sentence individually in their notebooks, blending the prefix to the given root to form the correct word. Teacher circulates, prompting children to say the blend aloud before writing.

Whole-class answer share: invite children to read each completed sentence. Confirm correct answers (stones, spoon, story, skirt) on the board. Correct any errors by saying the word slowly and asking children to hear the blend.

periods.teacher_notes: Children sometimes confuse 'sp' and 'st' when the root word begins with a vowel; model 'sp + oon = spoon' by blending slowly on the board. The sentence context gives a strong semantic cue — use it to help children self-check (a 'spoon' is needed with a 'bowl for soup').

periods.activity_title: Describing the Moon: Drawing and Writing

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us write — B (p.125): draw the Moon and write a few describing lines.

time_bands.activity: Teacher leads a brief oral brainstorm: 'What do you know or imagine about the Moon — its colour, shape, surface, how it looks at night?' Record three to four ideas on the board as a word bank (e.g. round, bright, silver, craters, dark patches).
Children draw their picture of the Moon in their notebooks, referring to the word bank and to what Nandini Aunty described in the story. Teacher circulates and encourages detail in the drawing.

Let us write — B ("draw the Moon and write descriptive lines, p.125"): children write two to three sentences about their drawing, using the word bank and a sentence frame on the board: 'The Moon looks ___. It is ___. I think the Moon ___.' Teacher supports children who need help forming sentences.
Gallery share: children hold up their drawings and read their sentences aloud to a partner. Teacher selects two or three to share with the class, celebrating vivid describing words.

periods.teacher_notes: The writing task connects directly to Rani's wonder about the Moon — children are essentially answering in writing the question Rani first asked her mother. Provide a simple sentence frame on the board so children who are less confident can begin writing quickly rather than stalling at the blank page.
materials: Notebooks, pencils, and crayons or coloured pencils
Board for word bank and sentence frame

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us learn (p.124): fill blanks using 'a' or 'an' in three exercise sets.

time_bands.activity: Write the two story sentences from the textbook on the board: 'There was a girl named Rani' and 'A hanky for an elephant.' Underline 'a' and 'an'. Ask children: why 'a girl' but 'an elephant'? Elicit the vowel-sound rule together.

Teacher models the rule clearly: 'a' before consonant sounds, 'an' before vowel sounds (a, e, i, o, u). Practise with quick oral examples — 'a dog / an eagle' — children call out the correct article as teacher shows a word.

Let us learn — A and B (p.124): ("fill blanks using 'a' only, then 'an' only"). Children complete the two sets individually in their notebooks. Teacher circulates and asks children to say the word aloud before writing to confirm the starting sound.

Let us learn — C (p.124): ("fill blanks choosing between 'a' and 'an' in mixed sentences"). Children attempt these more challenging items. Teacher pauses for 'An ice-cream man' to discuss 'an' before a vowel sound even when the word is compound.
Quick oral check: teacher reads each sentence starter and children call out the correct article in chorus. Confirm answers on the board.

periods.teacher_notes: The rule is introduced through the story's own language — Rani being 'a girl' and 'an elephant' being the textbook's own anchor sentences; return to these when children hesitate. Watch for 'an uniform' or 'an university' type errors, which reveal focus on spelling rather than sound — model the spoken word to redirect.

periods.activity_title: Days of the Week: Fun with Words

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Fun with Words — A and B (p.126): read days aloud and match each day to its ordinal position.

time_bands.activity: Teacher reads the seven sentences about the days of the week aloud (p.126) with the class following. Then the class reads them together in chorus, clapping on the ordinal word each time ('first', 'second', 'third' …).

Fun with Words — A ("choral read-aloud of days-of-the-week sentences, p.126"): children read independently, running a finger along each line. Teacher moves around to check pronunciation of 'Wednesday' and the ordinals 'third', 'fourth', 'fifth'.

Fun with Words — B ("match each day to its ordinal position in a week, p.126"): children complete the matching exercise in their notebooks, using the text as a reference. Teacher prompts: 'Find the sentence that mentions Monday — what ordinal does it use?'
Pair-check: children swap notebooks and verify each other's answers against the text. Confirm the full sequence on the board: Sunday–first through Saturday–seventh.
Quick game: teacher calls a day, children call back the ordinal number — speed and enthusiasm encouraged. Reverse the game: teacher calls an ordinal, children call the day.

periods.teacher_notes: Ordinal numbers ('first' through 'seventh') may be new language for some children at Grade III; the text is self-referential and children can look up any answer directly from the sentences on the page, which makes this a supported word-game rather than a memory test. The game in the final band reinforces fluency through play.

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us do — A (p.127): collect and arrange Chandrayaan-3 clippings on chart paper for display.

time_bands.activity: Teacher briefly recalls the story's key facts — Chandrayaan-3 was launched 14 July 2023 and landed 23 August 2023 — and explains that these events were reported in newspapers and magazines around the world. Show the class an example clipping or a printed image if available.

Divide the class into small groups. Each group receives chart paper, glue, scissors, and any clippings or printed materials brought in. Groups plan the layout of their display: a title area, picture area, and a caption area.

Let us do — A ("group Chandrayaan-3 clippings display on chart paper, p.127"): groups cut, arrange, and paste their clippings. Each group writes a short title (e.g. 'India on the Moon!') and one-sentence caption under at least one image.
Groups display their charts and take turns presenting one fact or image to the class in one or two sentences. Celebrate each group's effort; post the charts in the classroom.

periods.teacher_notes: If children have not brought clippings, teacher can pre-print two or three images of the Chandrayaan-3 lander and rocket for each group. The captions children write are a light writing task embedded in the project — encourage complete sentences rather than single words.
materials: Newspaper or magazine clippings (or teacher-printed images)

periods.activity_title: Moon Songs and Stories: Let Us Explore

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us explore — A (p.127): share a moon song or story from your mother tongue with the class.

time_bands.activity: Teacher recalls the opening of the story — Rani's mother singing 'Chanda mama door ke …' — and asks children whether they know any song, rhyme, or story about the Moon from their home language. Allow a moment of quiet recall.

Let us explore — A ("share a moon song or story from mother tongue, p.127"): children take turns sharing. Each child sings, recites, or tells their moon item in their home language, then gives a brief explanation of what it means in English. Teacher participates warmly and models if a child is shy.

Teacher leads the class in a unison chant of 'Chanda mama door ke' (from the story), then invites the class to hum or tap a rhythm together. Discuss: why do people all over India have songs and stories about the Moon?
Brief reflection: children name one thing they found interesting or surprising in a classmate's moon song or story. Teacher affirms the diversity of traditions represented in the room.

periods.teacher_notes: The task is rooted in the story's opening lullaby and celebrates multilingualism — every child's contribution is valid regardless of the language. Children who did not find a moon song at home may share any family story involving the Moon or night sky.

time_bands.activity: Teacher-led recall: ask children to retell the story of Chandrayaan in their own words — who the characters were, what question Rani asked, and what Nandini Aunty explained. Accept oral contributions from several children to build the full narrative aloud together.

Oracy round-table: pairs take two minutes to tell each other — as if speaking to a younger sibling — what Chandrayaan-3 is and why it matters. Then a few pairs share their retelling with the class. Teacher notes especially clear or vivid retellings.

Independent writing: each child writes three sentences in their notebook — one about what Chandrayaan-3 did, one using 'a' or 'an' correctly in a sentence about space, and one describing what they would say to Rani if they met her. Teacher circulates to support.

Word-work quick game: teacher calls a noun from the story (eagle, astronaut, rocket, uniform) and children call back the correct article. Then children compose one new 'a / an' sentence of their own, using a space-related word.

Closing celebration: the class chants 'Chanda mama door ke' together, then in chorus says: 'Chandrayaan-3 landed on the Moon on 23 August 2023 — India reached the Moon!' Teacher invites children to ask one lingering question about space that Rani might have asked.

periods.teacher_notes: This unit draws together the story's characters and events, the articles 'a' and 'an', the theme of scientific curiosity, and the cultural moon traditions children explored — all named content from the chapter. The writing task is brief by design so that drafting, peer reading, and revision all complete within the sitting.

items.item_stem: Read the sentences below. Write TRUE if the sentence is correct according to the story of Chandrayaan, or FALSE if it is not.

options.text: It was Rani who told her brother about India landing on the Moon.
Nandini Aunty is a scientist and Vivaan's mother.
Rani's mother was singing about the Moon when Rani asked how far the Moon is.

teacher_guide.suggested_answer: 1 — True (Rani heard her mother sing 'Chanda mama door ke' and then asked about the Moon's distance). 2 — False (it was Pratik who excitedly pointed to the TV news about India landing on the Moon, not Rani). 3 — True (Nandini Aunty is described as a scientist and as Vivaan's mother). 4 — False ('Chandrayaan' means Moon vehicle: 'Chandra' means Moon and 'Yaan' means vehicle).

items.item_stem: In the story, Rani is described as a very curious girl. Write two to three sentences explaining how the story shows that Rani is curious. Use something she says or does in your answer.

teacher_guide.suggested_answer: Rani constantly asks questions about the world around her. When she hears her mother singing about the Moon, she immediately asks how far the Moon is, showing she wants to understand things she does not know.

items.item_stem: Nandini Aunty told Rani that she might one day travel to the Moon. If you were going to spend ten days on the Moon, which THREE items would you most want to take, and why? Choose from the list below.

options.label: A
options.text: A notebook, a pencil, and a hat

options.label: B
options.text: A pair of shoes, a blanket, and a flower pot

options.label: C
options.text: A television, a bicycle, and a kite

options.label: D
options.text: Food, water, and an oxygen tank

what_each_option_reveals.C: A child who picks this may be focused on entertainment rather than survival needs in space.
what_each_option_reveals.A: This suggests the child is thinking of classroom items rather than the practical demands of a space journey.
what_each_option_reveals.B: A child who picks this may not yet be connecting the Moon's airless, extreme environment to basic survival needs.
